newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - European stocks surge on Greenspan comments.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - European stocks surge on Greenspan comments.

text.p: European stock markets powered ahead on Wednesday after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan sent Wall Street to a record by indicating U.S. interest rates would not rise soon.
In early trading the German market, which already hit a record high on Tuesday, rocketed three percent while Paris gained about 2.5 percent and London rose 1.5 percent.

Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress on Tuesday was devoid of any mentions of market bubbles and irrational exuberance, the sort of comments that sent financial markets reeling last December.
But, speaking after European markets closed, Greenspan was cautious in his comments.
"I have no doubt that the current stance of policy...will need to be changed at some point," he said in prepared testimony to a House Banking subcommittee.
"For the present, as I indicated, demand growth does appear to have moderated, but whether that moderation will be sufficient to avoid putting additional pressures on resources is an open question."
Wall Street, hit by profit taking in recent sessions, saw Greenspan's comments as the green light to buy.

The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 154.93 points, or 1.96 percent, to 8,061.65, beating last Wednesday's record finish of 8,038.88. It was also the Dow's fourth biggest gain in history.
Germany was the star performer again, with the IBIS index of electronic trading up 131.18 points or 3.05 percent at 4,428.82. The banking and motor industry sectors perfomerd particularly strongly.

"The banks are up, the cars are up. The DTB options guys are starting to buy. Everything is good as gold as far as I can see," a Frankfurt trader said. A strong dollar trading around 1.82 marks underpinned sentiment.

Monday's news that Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypobank would merge had already fired up investors, believing that a long-awaited consolidation of the fragmented banking sector might be under way.

Germany's largest bank, Deutsche Bank AG helped sentiment by reporting a 27.5 percent rise in net income. The result, above forecasts, sent its shares surging more than five percent to an all-time high.
In London, the FTSE-100 index gained 74.3 points or 1.53 percent to 4,921.0.
But NatWest markets UK strategist David McBain noted that Greenspan would address the Senate banking committee on Wednesday in the second leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony at 1400 GMT.
"We're not quite out of the woods with the second part of Greenspan's testimony this afternoon. Greenspan may try to temper the markets' reaction," he said.
In Paris the CAC-40 index jumped 72.24 points or 2.47 percent to 2,993.37.
On the foreign exchange markets, the dollar made a strong start against the mark in Europe, buoyed from its overnight gains by Greenspan's comments that, for now, U.S. growth seemed to be slowing.

"Greenspan has painted a very nice picture of the U.S. economy which is very bullish for U.S. asset markets," said Jesper Dannesboe, treasury economist at ABN-Amro in London. "The strong growth and low inflation scenario is also quite bullish for the dollar."
The dollar's recent break above 1.82 marks has re-ignited some concern of central bank intervention but this is less likely now than a week ago when the dollar wrestled with the key 1.80 mark level.

"No doubt we will get the German authorities saying they are in contact with their G7 partners, but central banks are more astute and intervention now would be as effective as whistling against the wind," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets in London.

The dollar was trading at 1.8259 marks against 1.8173 late Tuesday in Europe and after climbing to 1.8245 in New York trade, its highest level since August 1991. It calmed down in Asian trade but climbed again in Europe.
As well as the Greenspan factor, the dollar continued to find support from the general mark weakness and the continuing uncertainty over European monetary union.

"With structural problems remaining untackled in Europe, the higher dollar will find few opponents on this side of the Atlantic," said Michael Lewis, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
